flexCountReg

The goal of flexCountReg is to provide functions that allow the analyst to estimate count regression models that can handle multiple analysis issues, including:

  • many count distributions beyond the Poisson and negative binomial (see the list below), with any distribution parameter modeled as a function of variables (generalized count models);
  • underreporting, and zero-inflated or hurdle versions of every distribution;
  • random parameters, with heterogeneity in their means and variances, and exact, simulated and Empirical Bayes (observation-specific) predictions;
  • random-effects panel models (negative binomial, Poisson-Lindley, negative multinomial);
  • model comparison and diagnostics: likelihood-ratio tests, comparison tables, marginal effects, CURE plots, rootograms and randomized quantile residuals.

Fitted models work with the standard R generics (coef(), vcov(), AIC(), BIC(), confint(), predict(), simulate(), update(), …), with tidy(), glance() and augment(), and with tidymodels through the count_reg() parsnip model.

Installation

You can install the development version of flexCountReg using:

# install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("jwood-iastate/flexCountReg")

Functions and Data

Model Estimation Functions

  • countreg() estimates cross-sectional count regression models with any of the distributions below, optional models for the distribution parameters, underreporting, and zero-inflated or hurdle zero models.
  • countreg.rp() (also countreg_rp()) estimates random parameters count models, optionally with panels, correlated random parameters, and heterogeneity in the means and variances of the random parameters.
  • renb() estimates the random effects negative binomial regression model.
  • poisLind.re() (also poislind_re()) estimates the random effects Poisson-Lindley model.
  • negmultinom() estimates negative multinomial (random effects) panel models (NM1, NM2 and NM-P).
  • repois() estimates the random effects Poisson model with a gamma random effect.
  • count_reg() is a parsnip model specification with a "flexCountReg" engine, for use with tidymodels (the distribution can be tuned with count_family()).

Working with Fitted Models

  • summary() gives the coefficient table, standard-error type, fit statistics and a likelihood-ratio test against the Poisson model.
  • predict() gives expected counts (one per row of newdata, NA for incomplete rows), the probability of each count, and the components of underreporting and zero models. For countreg() models it also gives confidence intervals for the expected count and prediction intervals for a new count (interval = "confidence" or "prediction"). For random parameters models it offers exact, simulated and Empirical Bayes ("Individual") predictions.
  • tolerance_interval() gives content tolerance intervals for countreg() models: count ranges intended to contain at least a stated share of the outcome distribution with a stated confidence.
  • coef(), vcov(), confint(), logLik(), AIC(), BIC(), nobs(), fitted(), residuals() (response, Pearson and randomized quantile), simulate() and update() work as for other R models.
  • tidy(), glance() and augment() return tibbles in the broom format.

Model Evaluation, Comparison, and Convenience Functions

  • regCompTest() compares a model with a base model, or two fitted models, with a likelihood ratio test, AIC, BIC and McFadden’s pseudo R-squared.
  • regCompTable() creates a publication-ready table comparing multiple models.
  • margEffTable() computes marginal effects (or elasticities) with delta-method or bootstrap standard errors.
  • cureplot() generates a CURE plot for the specified model, based on the cureplots package.
  • rootogram() compares observed and expected count frequencies.
  • mae() and rmse() compute the mean absolute error and root mean squared error; myAIC() and myBIC() compute AIC and BIC from a log-likelihood.
  • halton_dists(), corr_haltons() and cor2cov() generate (correlated) Halton draws and convert correlation matrices to covariance matrices.

Distribution Functions

Density (d), distribution (p), quantile (q) and random generation (r) functions are provided for each distribution:

Count distributions

  • Conway-Maxwell-Poisson (COM): dcom, pcom, qcom, rcom
  • Delaporte: ddelaporte, pdelaporte, qdelaporte, rdelaporte
  • Discrete Weibull: ddweib, pdweib, qdweib, rdweib
  • Double Poisson: ddpo, pdpo, qdpo, rdpo
  • Gamma Count: dgcount, pgcount, qgcount, rgcount
  • Generalized Hermite: dghermite, pghermite, qghermite, rghermite
  • Generalized Poisson Version 1: dgp1, pgp1, qgp1, rgp1
  • Generalized Poisson Version 2: dgp2, pgp2, qgp2, rgp2
  • Generalized Waring: dgwar, pgwar, qgwar, rgwar
  • Hyper-Poisson: dhpois, phpois, qhpois, rhpois
  • Negative Binomial-Generalized Exponential: dnbge, pnbge, qnbge, rnbge
  • Poisson-Generalized-Exponential: dpge, ppge, qpge, rpge
  • Poisson-Inverse-Gamma: dpinvgamma, ppinvgamma, qpinvgamma, rpinvgamma
  • Poisson-Inverse-Gaussian: dpinvgaus, ppinvgaus, qpinvgaus, rpinvgaus
  • Poisson-Lindley: dplind, pplind, qplind, rplind
  • Poisson-Lindley-Gamma (Negative Binomial-Lindley): dplindGamma, pplindGamma, qplindGamma, rplindGamma
  • Poisson-Lindley-Lognormal: dplindLnorm, pplindLnorm, qplindLnorm, rplindLnorm
  • Poisson-Lognormal: dpLnorm, ppLnorm, qpLnorm, rpLnorm
  • Poisson-Weibull: dpoisweibull, ppoisweibull, qpoisweibull, rpoisweibull
  • Polya-Aeppli: dpaeppli, ppaeppli, qpaeppli, rpaeppli
  • Sichel: dsichel, psichel, qsichel, rsichel

See ?count_families for every distribution available in countreg() and countreg.rp(), with its parameters, variance and model features.

Continuous distributions

  • Inverse Gamma: dinvgamma, pinvgamma, qinvgamma, rinvgamma
  • Inverse Gaussian: rinvgaus
  • Lindley: dlindley, plindley, qlindley, rlindley
  • Triangular: dtri, ptri, qtri, rtri
  • Lognormal: moment_lognormal for the moments of the lognormal distribution

Data

Three datasets are included:

  • washington_roads: a sample of Washington primary 2-lane roads from the years 2016-2018 (507 road segments, each observed in up to three years). Data for the roads, traffic volumes (AADT) and associated crashes were obtained from the Highway Safety Information System (HSIS).
  • abalone_rings: shell-ring counts and physical measurements of 4,177 abalone from the UCI Machine Learning Repository (CC BY 4.0), a non-transportation example with conditionally underdispersed counts.
  • stream_salamanders: repeated counts of seven stream salamander groups at 23 sites in Kentucky (Price et al., 2016; Dryad, CC0), zero-heavy, overdispersed and grouped by site.

Probability Distributions

As noted in the list of functions, the probability distributions below are included in the flexCountReg package. Details of the distributions are provided in the documentation (help files).

Continuous Distributions

  • Inverse Gamma Distribution
  • Triangle Distribution

Count Distributions Distributions that Handle Equidispersion

  • Poisson

Distributions that handle Underdispersion (and Overdispersion)

  • Conway-Maxwell-Poisson (COM) Distribution
  • Generalized Poisson Distribution (Types 1 and 2)
  • Discrete Weibull Distribution
  • Double Poisson Distribution
  • Hyper-Poisson Distribution
  • Gamma Count (Renewal) Distribution

Distributions that Handle Overdispersion

  • Negative Binomial in various forms (NB-1, NB-2, and NB-P)
  • Poisson-Inverse-Gaussian Distribution (Types 1 and 2)
  • Poisson-Inverse-Gamma
  • Poisson-Lognormal Distribution
  • Poisson-Weibull Distribution
  • Sichel Distribution
  • Generalized Waring Distribution
  • Delaporte Distribution
  • Hermite Distribution (orders 2, 3 and 4; bounded overdispersion)
  • Polya-Aeppli (Poisson-Tweedie, power 1.5) Distribution

Distributions that Handle Higher Densities of Zeros and Overdispersion

  • Poisson-Generalized-Exponential Distribution
  • Poisson-Lindley Distribution
  • Poisson-Lindley-Gamma (Negative Binomial-Lindley) Distribution
  • Poisson-Lindley-Lognormal Distribution
  • Negative Binomial-Generalized Exponential (NBGE) Distribution

Example

The following is an example of using flexCountReg to estimate a negative binomial (NB-2) regression model with the overdispersion parameter as a function of predictor variables:

library(flexCountReg)

data("washington_roads")
washington_roads$AADT10kplus <- ifelse(washington_roads$AADT > 10000, 1, 0)
gen.nb2 <- countreg(Total_crashes ~ lnaadt + lnlength + speed50,
                    data = washington_roads, family = "NB2",
                    dis_param_formula_1 = ~ speed50, method = "BFGS")
summary(gen.nb2)
#> Call:
#> countreg(formula = Total_crashes ~ lnaadt + lnlength + speed50, 
#>     data = washington_roads, family = "NB2", dis_param_formula_1 = ~speed50, 
#>     method = "BFGS")
#> 
#> Model: countreg | family: NB2 | optimizer: BFGS
#> Iterations: 40 
#> Convergence: successful convergence 
#> 
#> Coefficients (standard errors: Hessian-based):
#>                       Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
#> (Intercept)            -8.7564     0.4404  -19.88  < 2e-16 ***
#> lnaadt                  1.0803     0.0518   20.86  < 2e-16 ***
#> lnlength                0.7588     0.0691   10.98  < 2e-16 ***
#> speed50                -0.5407     0.1173   -4.61  4.0e-06 ***
#> ln(alpha):(Intercept)  -1.3233     0.3150   -4.20  2.7e-05 ***
#> ln(alpha):speed50       1.2670     0.4849    2.61    0.009 ** 
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Log-likelihood: -1082.176 | AIC: 2176.352 | BIC: 2208.235 
#> N: 1501

The results are also available as tibbles, and the model can be compared with a Poisson base model:

tidy(gen.nb2, conf.int = TRUE)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 8
#>   term        component estimate std.error statistic  p.value conf.low conf.high
#>   <chr>       <chr>        <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 (Intercept) mean        -8.76     0.440     -19.9  5.78e-88   -9.62     -7.89 
#> 2 lnaadt      mean         1.08     0.0518     20.9  1.23e-96    0.979     1.18 
#> 3 lnlength    mean         0.759    0.0691     11.0  4.63e-28    0.623     0.894
#> 4 speed50     mean        -0.541    0.117      -4.61 4.02e- 6   -0.771    -0.311
#> 5 ln(alpha):… distribu…   -1.32     0.315      -4.20 2.66e- 5   -1.94     -0.706
#> 6 ln(alpha):… distribu…    1.27     0.485       2.61 8.98e- 3    0.317     2.22
glance(gen.nb2)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 10
#>   model    family logLik   AIC   BIC    df  nobs n_groups converged vcov_type
#>   <chr>    <chr>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <int> <int>    <int> <lgl>     <chr>    
#> 1 countreg NB2    -1082. 2176. 2208.     6  1501       NA TRUE      hessian
regCompTest(gen.nb2, basemodel = "Poisson", variables = TRUE)$statistics
#> No LR test: the POISSON base model is not nested in the fitted model with a regular restriction (the restriction sets ln(alpha) to its boundary, which is not regular when ln(alpha) has a formula). Compare the models with AIC and BIC.
#> # A tibble: 8 × 3
#>   Statistic                  Model BaseModel
#>   <chr>                      <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 Log-likelihood        -1082.        -1101.
#> 2 Number of parameters      6             4 
#> 3 AIC                    2176.         2209.
#> 4 BIC                    2208.         2230.
#> 5 LR Test Statistic        NA            NA 
#> 6 LR degrees of freedom    NA            NA 
#> 7 LR p-value               NA            NA 
#> 8 McFadden's Pseudo R^2     0.0167       NA

A rootogram shows how well the fitted distribution reproduces the observed counts; bars that end above or below zero show counts that are over- or under-predicted:

pois <- update(gen.nb2, family = "Poisson", dis_param_formula_1 = NULL)
oldpar <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
rootogram(pois, main = "Poisson")
rootogram(gen.nb2, main = "Generalized NB-2")

par(oldpar)

Checking the CURE plot:

cureplot(gen.nb2, indvar = "lnaadt")
#> Covariate: indvar_values
#> CURE data frame was provided. Its first column, lnaadt, will be used.

Modifying the model:

gen.nb2 <- countreg(Total_crashes ~ lnaadt + lnlength + speed50 +
                      ShouldWidth04 + AADT10kplus + I(AADT10kplus / lnaadt),
                    data = washington_roads, family = "NB2",
                    dis_param_formula_1 = ~ lnlength, method = "BFGS")
summary(gen.nb2)
#> Call:
#> countreg(formula = Total_crashes ~ lnaadt + lnlength + speed50 + 
#>     ShouldWidth04 + AADT10kplus + I(AADT10kplus/lnaadt), data = washington_roads, 
#>     family = "NB2", dis_param_formula_1 = ~lnlength, method = "BFGS")
#> 
#> Model: countreg | family: NB2 | optimizer: BFGS
#> Iterations: 51 
#> Convergence: successful convergence 
#> 
#> Coefficients (standard errors: Hessian-based):
#>                       Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
#> (Intercept)            -7.6756     0.4877  -15.74  < 2e-16 ***
#> lnaadt                  0.9296     0.0569   16.32  < 2e-16 ***
#> lnlength                0.8534     0.0699   12.21  < 2e-16 ***
#> speed50                -0.3999     0.1091   -3.67  0.00025 ***
#> ShouldWidth04           0.2606     0.0916    2.84  0.00446 ** 
#> AADT10kplus             5.9613     4.5117    1.32  0.18640    
#> I(AADT10kplus/lnaadt) -50.1377    43.0019   -1.17  0.24364    
#> ln(alpha):(Intercept)  -1.9126     0.6648   -2.88  0.00401 ** 
#> ln(alpha):lnlength     -0.4301     0.4991   -0.86  0.38880    
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Log-likelihood: -1061.914 | AIC: 2141.828 | BIC: 2189.653 
#> N: 1501
cureplot(gen.nb2, indvar = "lnaadt")
#> Covariate: indvar_values
#> CURE data frame was provided. Its first column, lnaadt, will be used.

Estimating another model (NB-P), without the interaction:

gen.nbp <- countreg(Total_crashes ~ lnaadt + lnlength + speed50 +
                      ShouldWidth04 + AADT10kplus,
                    data = washington_roads, family = "NBP",
                    dis_param_formula_1 = ~ lnlength, method = "BFGS")
summary(gen.nbp)
#> Call:
#> countreg(formula = Total_crashes ~ lnaadt + lnlength + speed50 + 
#>     ShouldWidth04 + AADT10kplus, data = washington_roads, family = "NBP",

Checking the CURE plot (notice that the CURE plot is better in this case than the NB-2 without the interaction and still better than the modified NB-2):

cureplot(gen.nbp, indvar = "lnaadt")
#> Covariate: indvar_values
#> CURE data frame was provided. Its first column, lnaadt, will be used.

Creating a table to compare the models:

regCompTable(list("Generalized NB-2" = gen.nb2, "Generalized NB-P" = gen.nbp))
#> # A tibble: 15 × 3
#>    Parameter             `Generalized NB-2` `Generalized NB-P`
#>    <chr>                 <chr>              <chr>             
#>  1 (Intercept)           -7.676 (0.488)***  -7.764 (0.485)*** 
#>  2 lnaadt                0.93 (0.057)***    0.938 (0.057)***  
#>  3 lnlength              0.853 (0.07)***    0.836 (0.07)***   
#>  4 speed50               -0.4 (0.109)***    -0.384 (0.111)*** 
#>  5 ShouldWidth04         0.261 (0.092)**    0.258 (0.092)**   
#>  6 AADT10kplus           5.961 (4.512)      0.689 (0.132)***  
#>  7 I(AADT10kplus/lnaadt) -50.138 (43.002)   ---               
#>  8 ln(alpha):(Intercept) -1.913 (0.665)**   -1.496 (0.535)**  
#>  9 ln(alpha):lnlength    -0.43 (0.499)      -0.167 (0.445)    
#> 10 ln(p)                 ---                0.525 (0.184)**   
#> 11 N Obs.                1501               1501              
#> 12 LL                    -1061.914          -1062.195         
#> 13 AIC                   2141.828           2142.389          
#> 14 BIC                   2189.653           2190.214          
#> 15 Pseudo-R-Sq.          0.303              0.303

Note that the metrics for comparison are similar. While the models both have the same number of parameters, the NB-P was able to get better performance without requiring the interaction terms (which leads to strange relationships between the exposure metric and the outcome).

Predictions have one value per row of new data, and the probability of each count is also available:

nd <- washington_roads[1:3, ]
predict(gen.nbp, newdata = nd)
#> [1] 0.6417932 0.5787698 0.8832648
round(predict(gen.nbp, newdata = nd, type = "prob", max_count = 4), 3)
#>          0     1     2     3     4
#> [1,] 0.556 0.300 0.105 0.030 0.008
#> [2,] 0.587 0.288 0.093 0.025 0.006
#> [3,] 0.450 0.326 0.147 0.053 0.017

Zero-inflated and hurdle versions of any distribution are fitted with zero_formula. For example, animal-related crashes are zero on most segment-years, and a zero-inflated Poisson model with the zero probability depending on the speed limit can be compared with the Poisson model by AIC and BIC (not by a likelihood-ratio test: no zero inflation puts the zero model’s intercept at minus infinity, so the restriction is not regular):

mean(washington_roads$Animal == 0)
#> [1] 0.9540306
zip <- countreg(Animal ~ lnaadt + lnlength, data = washington_roads,
                family = "Poisson", zero_formula = ~ speed50, method = "NR")
tidy(zip)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 6
#>   term             component estimate std.error statistic  p.value
#>   <chr>            <chr>        <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1 (Intercept)      mean        -8.64      1.17     -7.41  1.26e-13
#> 2 lnaadt           mean         0.976     0.134     7.28  3.33e-13
#> 3 lnlength         mean         1.53      0.212     7.21  5.52e-13
#> 4 Zero:(Intercept) zero        -0.116     0.482    -0.241 8.10e- 1
#> 5 Zero:speed50     zero         1.51      0.478     3.16  1.59e- 3
rbind(Poisson = glance(update(zip, zero_formula = NULL)),
      ZIP = glance(zip))[, c("logLik", "AIC", "BIC")]
#> # A tibble: 2 × 3
#>   logLik   AIC   BIC
#>    <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1  -278.  562.  578.
#> 2  -266.  542.  569.

With tidymodels (requires the parsnip package):

library(parsnip)
spec <- count_reg(family = "NB2") |> set_engine("flexCountReg", method = "BFGS")
fit <- fit(spec, Total_crashes ~ lnaadt + lnlength + speed50,
           data = washington_roads)
predict(fit, new_data = washington_roads[1:5, ])
